Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette: Rohan still recalls the day his life changed forever. He was 32 years old when he was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of leukemia. The months that followed were a blur of hospital visits, chemotherapy sessions, and endless tests. His body felt like it was under siege, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was running out of time. As he began to recover, Rohan started to notice a growing sense of unease within himself. He had always been an optimistic person, but now he found himself consumed by negative thoughts about his own worth. There is something wrong with me as a person, he would often think to himself. This feeling of being defective seeped into every aspect of his life, making him withdrawn and isolated. His fear of being weak and vulnerable also intensified. He became convinced that he was no longer capable of handling physical stress, and situations that put his body under strain made him anxious. Rohan started avoiding activities that he used to enjoy, like hiking or playing sports with friends. He even stopped going to the gym, fearing that any exertion would trigger a relapse. As these avoidance behaviors took hold, Rohan's perception of safety began to erode. Even when his loved ones reassured him that he was safe, he couldn't shake off the feeling that something bad was lurking around the corner. His wife would try to calm him down, saying "you're okay, you're in remission," but Rohan just couldn't trust it. He felt like his body was constantly on alert, tense and ready to react to danger at any moment. This sense of unease only grew stronger when things didn't go according to plan. When a project at work took longer than expected, Rohan would assume that something had gone terribly wrong. His mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios, and he would become convinced that his life was once again under threat. As the months went by, these patterns of thinking only intensified. Rohan started avoiding medical cues altogether – hospitals, ambulances, even physical examinations made him anxious. He stopped going for check-ups, fearing what the doctors might find. His avoidance behaviors became a self-reinforcing cycle: the more he avoided, the more he felt like he was in danger, and the more he felt like he was in danger, the more he avoided. Rohan's emotional numbness also deepened. He felt dead inside, like he was just going through the motions of daily life without any real purpose or passion. His relationships suffered as a result – his wife felt like she was losing him, and his friends didn't know how to reach out. It was only when Rohan's avoidance behaviors started affecting his work that he realized he needed help. As a UX designer, he was used to being creative and problem-solving, but now he found himself struggling to meet deadlines and collaborate with colleagues. His fear of physical stress had become so debilitating that he couldn't even sit in front of a computer for more than an hour without feeling overwhelmed. Rohan finally sought therapy when his wife staged an intervention. She told him that she couldn't watch him slip away anymore, and that she needed her husband back. Rohan was afraid of what the future held, but he knew he had to face his fears head-on. He was tired of living in a state of constant threat, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. With therapy, he hoped to find a way to break free from this cycle of avoidance and fear, and rediscover the person he used to be.
